title: HalluciNot: Hallucination Detection Through Context and Common Knowledge Verification
abstract: This paper introduces a comprehensive system for detecting hallucinations in large language model (LLM) outputs in enterprise settings. We present a novel taxonomy of LLM responses specific to hallucination in enterprise applications, categorizing them into context-based, common knowledge, enterprise-specific, and innocuous statements. Our hallucination detection model HDM-2 validates LLM responses with respect to both context and generally known facts (common knowledge). It provides both hallucination scores and word-level annotations, enabling precise identification of problematic content. To evaluate it on context-based and common-knowledge hallucinations, we introduce a new dataset HDMBench. Experimental results demonstrate that HDM-2 out-performs existing approaches across RagTruth, TruthfulQA, and HDMBench datasets. This work addresses the specific challenges of enterprise deployment, including computational efficiency, domain specialization, and fine-grained error identification. Our evaluation dataset, model weights, and inference code are publicly available.

claims.text: HDM-2 achieves an overall F1 score of 85.03 on the RagTruth dataset for response-level context-based hallucination detection.
HDM-2 achieves an F1 score of 83.7 on the TruthfulQA dataset for common knowledge hallucination detection.
HDM-2 achieves an F1 score of 73.6 on the HDMBench dataset for common knowledge hallucination detection.
Common knowledge hallucination detection accuracy using Qwen-2.5-3B-Instruct internal representations peaks at intermediate layer 25.
HDM-2 uses Qwen-2.5-3B-Instruct as its pre-trained backbone model.
HDM-2 combines context-based verification and common knowledge detection into a single modular architecture.

limitations.text: Existing self-consistency methods require multiple model invocations or decoding-stage modifications, leading to high computational overhead and latency in production environments.

Representation-based detection techniques require direct access to internal activations, probability distributions, or internal states of the generating model, limiting applicability to black-box models.

The evaluation and model capability in this work are currently focused primarily on context-based and common knowledge hallucinations, leaving full integration of enterprise-specific knowledge, multilingual support, and adversarial robustness to future work.

future_work.text: Extend hallucination detection to cover other taxonomy categories, including proprietary enterprise-specific knowledge verification.
Improve computational efficiency, multilingual support, and adversarial robustness for the hallucination detection pipeline.

methodologies.name: HDM-2 Hallucination Detection Model
methodologies.description: A multi-task detection framework utilizing a fine-tuned backbone language model (Qwen-2.5-3B-Instruct) with token/sequence classification loss for context consistency and shallow classifiers on intermediate layer activations for common knowledge verification.

methodologies.name: HDMBench Dataset Generation Pipeline
methodologies.description: A multi-stage pipeline creating a benchmark dataset covering context-based, common knowledge, enterprise-specific, and innocuous statements using diverse generator LLMs and phrase-level annotations with DeepSeek R1.
